body: [{"streamId":"01a1fa2c-5c0c-77d1-8fed-c30724cc7578","eventTypeName":"Hall9k.Domain.Features.Tasks.Events.TaskAdded","eventDataJson":"{\u0022Id\u0022:\u002201a1fa2c-5c0c-77d1-8fed-c30724cc7578\u0022,\u0022ProjectId\u0022:\u002201a00d41-5d9a-73cc-b648-af431f721a71\u0022,\u0022Objective\u0022:\u0022Answering a catch-up request that names no stream and no sequence bound (the gap-fill and bootstrap shapes) resolves each stream\\u0027s ownership once, so its database work grows with the number of streams in the log and not with several lookups for every event.\u0022,\u0022AcceptanceCriteria\u0022:[\u0022In one EventCatchUpResponder.AnswerAsync call for a request with no ForStreamId and no SinceGlobalSequence, ownership is resolved at most once per distinct stream id, however many events that stream has. A test builds a log of N project-scoped events spread over K streams (N much larger than K), counts the resolutions or the database commands issued during the call, and asserts the count is bounded by K and does not grow with N. The test fails without the change.\u0022,\u0022The answer itself is unchanged. For a mixed log (a project stream, tasks, ideas, epics, runs, decisions and learnings, some private, some belonging to another project, some fleet-scoped), the envelopes queued by a bootstrap request and by a gap-fill request hold the same records in the same order and the same batches as before, including the events-unavailable and events-answer-complete envelopes. A test asserts this, and the existing EventCatchUpResponder tests pass unmodified.\u0022,\u0022Nothing resolved for one AnswerAsync call is reused by a later call. A test answers a request, changes a task\\u0027s scope from private to team, answers the same request again, and the second answer includes that task\\u0027s events.\u0022],\u0022Type\u0022:\u0022Bugfix\u0022,\u0022AgentContext\u0022:\u0022## Where this came from\\n\\nOn 2026-11-20 a teammate\\u0027s two nodes joined five projects this node belongs to. Each node sent this node several catch-up requests per project that name no stream and no global sequence bound (the gap-fill shape, one per origin node, and the bootstrap shape). This node\\u0027s event log held about 233,000 events at the time.\\n\\nAnswering the first four of those requests, all for one project, took 87 minutes, which is about 22 minutes per request. The daemon sat near 80% CPU for hours, and \\u0060pg_stat_activity\\u0060 showed almost nothing except point reads by id of \\u0060mt_doc_taskdetails\\u0060, \\u0060mt_doc_projectdetails\\u0060, \\u0060mt_doc_ideadetails\\u0060, \\u0060mt_doc_epicdetails\\u0060 and \\u0060mt_doc_rundetails\\u0060. About 45 more requests of the same shape were queued behind them. Because the message sweep is one sequential loop, no project on the node flushed or read any mail while this ran.\\n\\n## Where the cost is\\n\\n\\u0060EventCatchUpResponder.AnswerAsync\\u0060 (src/Hall9k.Connectors/Replication/EventCatchUpResponder.cs) builds its query from \\u0060session.Events.QueryAllRawEvents()\\u0060. When the request names a stream, or a global sequence bound, the query is narrowed. For the gap-fill and bootstrap shapes it is not, so the whole log is loaded and walked. The comment above the query already records that these two shapes \\u0022still need the full scan\\u0022.\\n\\nInside the loop, every project-scoped event calls \\u0060ReplicationProjectResolver.ResolveAsync(session, candidate, ...)\\u0060. That method (src/Hall9k.Connectors/Replication/ReplicationProjectResolver.cs) tries \\u0060LoadAsync\\u0060 for \\u0060ProjectDetails\\u0060, then \\u0060TaskDetails\\u0060, \\u0060IdeaDetails\\u0060, \\u0060EpicDetails\\u0060, \\u0060RunDetails\\u0060 (plus the run\\u0027s task), \\u0060DecisionDetails\\u0060 and \\u0060LearningDetails\\u0060 in turn, on a lightweight session, so nothing is remembered between calls. A run\\u0027s event costs five or six round trips, and the same stream is resolved again for each of its events.\\n\\nOwnership is a property of the stream, not of the event, for the purposes of this scan. Resolving each distinct stream id once per \\u0060AnswerAsync\\u0060 call would turn hundreds of thousands of lookups into a few thousand.\\n\\n## Boundaries\\n\\n- The content of an answer must not change: the same records, in the same ascending global-sequence order, in the same envelopes, with the same \\u0060events-unavailable\\u0060 and \\u0060events-answer-complete\\u0060 envelopes.\\n- The private exclusions, the project-identity exclusion, the switch-on exclusion and the fleet-scope match all stay exactly as they are.\\n- Any reuse of a resolved ownership is scoped to one \\u0060AnswerAsync\\u0060 call. Nothing is cached across calls, across requests, or across sweep ticks, since a task\\u0027s or an idea\\u0027s scope can change between them.\\n- \\u0060EventReplicationOutbox.QueuePendingAsync\\u0060 calls the same resolver per event. It normally scans a short tail, so it is not the target here. If the change lands in a shared place and covers it at no extra risk, say so in the pull request. Otherwise leave it alone.\\n- Narrowing the unbounded query in SQL (for example to project-scoped event types) may also be worth doing, but the observed cost was dominated by the per-event lookups, not by the load. Measure before adding it, and keep it out if it complicates the ordering guarantees.\\n- How the message sweep orders its work across projects is a separate task and is not part of this one.\u0022,\u0022Constraints\u0022:null,\u0022ExternalReference\u0022:null,\u0022AddedAt\u0022:\u00222026-11-20T18:16:13.585411\u002B00:00\u0022,\u0022AddedByOwnerId\u0022:\u002201a00d41-5a50-7368-b048-72bcfee948bf\u0022,\u0022Model\u0022:\u0022\u0022,\u0022BlockedBy\u0022:[],\u0022StartsAsDraft\u0022:true,\u0022SourceIdeaId\u0022:null,\u0022EpicId\u0022:null,\u0022ReviewStageComposition\u0022:null,\u0022ReviewStageCompositionAcknowledged\u0022:false,\u0022StackedOnTaskId\u0022:null,\u0022PreApproved\u0022:false,\u0022Origin\u0022:null,\u0022PreApproval\u0022:\u0022Off\u0022,\u0022StackedOnPullRequestNumber\u0022:null,\u0022SecondaryExternalReference\u0022:null,\u0022SpikeKind\u0022:null,\u0022ExitCriterion\u0022:null,\u0022InitialScope\u0022:\u0022Fleet\u0022,\u0022HumanGate\u0022:false,\u0022EvolvedFromTaskId\u0022:null}","originEventId":"d32540b5-e04d-45ae-9935-9ac86256c8b9","originSequence":232946,"originNodeId":"01a00d41-5b80-753d-a3f1-070b25e490e4","originOwnerRootFingerprint":"c8f5c85900dac9911ce1ada43484dc7bf91a2a3e86efa8812d9f84cfd25bf2ac","originAt":"2026-11-20T18:16:13.636036+00:00","originProjectId":"01a00d41-5d9a-73cc-b648-af431f721a71"},{"streamId":"01a1fa2c-5eb1-77d2-ab94-8d0c9e13f3c1","eventTypeName":"Hall9k.Domain.Features.Tasks.Events.TaskAdded","eventDataJson":"{\u0022Id\u0022:\u002201a1fa2c-5eb1-77d2-ab94-8d0c9e13f3c1\u0022,\u0022ProjectId\u0022:\u002201a00d41-5d9a-73cc-b648-af431f721a71\u0022,\u0022Objective\u0022:\u0022A slow inbound read in one project no longer delays any project\\u0027s sends: the message sweep flushes every eligible project\\u0027s queued envelopes before it reads any project\\u0027s mail, and envelopes a read queues are flushed before the sweep moves on to the next project\\u0027s read.\u0022,\u0022AcceptanceCriteria\u0022:[\u0022With two eligible projects A and B, A earlier in id order, both holding pending envelopes, and A\\u0027s inbound read made to block through a test seam, B\\u0027s pending envelopes are flushed in that tick before A\\u0027s read completes. An integration test covers this and fails without the change, because B\\u0027s flush waits behind A\\u0027s read.\u0022,\u0022When a project\\u0027s read queues new envelopes in a tick (for example a catch-up answer), those envelopes are flushed in the same tick, before the next project\\u0027s read begins. An integration test covers this and fails without the change, because the answer stays unsent until the next tick reaches that project.\u0022,\u0022A failure in one project\\u0027s flush or read still leaves every other project\\u0027s flush and read in that tick unaffected, and MessageSweepResult.JustPushed and ActiveCadence read as they do today for a tick with no slow read. The existing MessageSweepEngine tests pass, changed only where they assert the old per-project ordering.\u0022],\u0022Type\u0022:\u0022Bugfix\u0022,\u0022AgentContext\u0022:\u0022## Where this came from\\n\\nOn 2026-11-20 this node spent hours answering whole-history catch-up requests from a teammate\\u0027s two newly joined nodes (the cost of one answer is its own task). The way the message sweep orders its work turned that slow step into a node-wide stall:\\n\\n- \\u0060MessageSweepEngine.SweepOnceAsync\\u0060 (src/Hall9k.Daemon/Messaging/MessageSweepEngine.cs) walks the eligible projects in id order, and for each one runs queue, flush, probe-and-read, then squash before it moves to the next project.\\n- Probe-and-read is where inbound catch-up requests are answered. One project\\u0027s read ran for 87 minutes. Every project later in id order waited that long for its own flush, and every project earlier in id order waited for the whole tick to end.\\n- A member vouch this node had recorded at 10:29 for a project late in the order was still unflushed three hours later, so the vouched teammate\\u0027s nodes kept showing that project as not joined.\\n- Answers queued during a project\\u0027s read are only flushed when the next tick reaches that project again. Seven finished answer envelopes for one project sat unsent for hours while the same tick worked on other projects.\\n- The node\\u0027s unrelated projects were held up as well. Nothing was flushed or read for any of them for the length of the tick.\\n\\n## What is wanted\\n\\nA slow read in one project must not hold back sends for any project, and finished answers must not wait for a whole further tick.\\n\\nThe shape proposed here is a tick in two passes: first queue and flush every eligible project, then read each project, flushing a project again straight after its read when that read queued anything. This is a proposal, not a ruling. If bounding how much answering one tick may do per project turns out to be the better tool, say so before building it. The outcome in the criteria is what matters.\\n\\n## Boundaries\\n\\n- Each project keeps its own failure isolation: a failure in one project\\u0027s flush or read still never blocks or corrupts another project\\u0027s sweep.\\n- The legacy-adoption rules in the flush (the lowest eligible project id, and \\u0060legacyAlreadyClaimedThisTick\\u0060) keep their current meaning.\\n- \\u0060MessageSweepResult.JustPushed\\u0060 and \\u0060ActiveCadence\\u0060 keep their current meaning for the loop\\u0027s cadence.\\n- The trust chain computed for a project in a tick is still the one its own read uses in that tick.\\n- This task does not change what an answer contains or what it costs to build.\u0022,\u0022Constraints\u0022:null,\u0022ExternalReference\u0022:null,\u0022AddedAt\u0022:\u00222026-11-20T18:16:14.262791\u002B00:00\u0022,\u0022AddedByOwnerId\u0022:\u002201a00d41-5a50-7368-b048-72bcfee948bf\u0022,\u0022Model\u0022:\u0022\u0022,\u0022BlockedBy\u0022:[],\u0022StartsAsDraft\u0022:true,\u0022SourceIdeaId\u0022:null,\u0022EpicId\u0022:null,\u0022ReviewStageComposition\u0022:null,\u0022ReviewStageCompositionAcknowledged\u0022:false,\u0022StackedOnTaskId\u0022:null,\u0022PreApproved\u0022:false,\u0022Origin\u0022:null,\u0022PreApproval\u0022:\u0022Off\u0022,\u0022StackedOnPullRequestNumber\u0022:null,\u0022SecondaryExternalReference\u0022:null,\u0022SpikeKind\u0022:null,\u0022ExitCriterion\u0022:null,\u0022InitialScope\u0022:\u0022Fleet\u0022,\u0022HumanGate\u0022:false,\u0022EvolvedFromTaskId\u0022:null}","originEventId":"112df7d3-cc6f-413c-8313-1c3c934c250c","originSequence":232947,"originNodeId":"01a00d41-5b80-753d-a3f1-070b25e490e4","originOwnerRootFingerprint":"c8f5c85900dac9911ce1ada43484dc7bf91a2a3e86efa8812d9f84cfd25bf2ac","originAt":"2026-11-20T18:16:14.315283+00:00","originProjectId":"01a00d41-5d9a-73cc-b648-af431f721a71"}]
